mappings.note: Four observations of metals in dilute HCl explained by the reactivity series -- displacement identified from observation, the core of LO-1. The temperature rise in (b) is incidental.
Identify A from clues and 'write the chemical reactions involved' -- the equation is the assessed product, so C 1.3-LO-1 rather than the classification outcome.

Dark bottle for AgCl turns on photolytic decomposition. LO-1 covers decomposition; C 1.2-LO-2 rejected because no corrosion or rancidity is involved despite the stored 'Corrosion of silver and copper' tag.
Two explicit instructions: balance (C 1.3-LO-1) and classify (C 1.2-LO-1). The equations themselves are missing from the stored stem but the outcomes are stated in the instruction line.
Formulae of X and Y plus balanced equations for their reaction with water. Equation writing dominates; the burning observation only supplies the identities.
Zinc versus copper with dilute HCl: whether a displacement occurs. LO-1's displacement clause, not LO-2 -- nothing here is about corrosion.
Silver tarnishing named as corrosion and the black Ag2S identified -- LO-2's corrosion-of-metals clause exactly.
Part (a) wants the balanced equation with states, part (c) wants the reaction type. Part (d) asks a pH range, for which this frame has no outcome, so it is left uncited.

Characteristic laboratory tests for CO2, SO2, O2 and H2. No learning outcome in this frame covers gas identification tests -- LO-1 is about classifying reactions, C 8.1-LO-1 about the (g) symbol -- so the competency 'investigates the nature and properties of chemical substances' is the honest level.
Predicts whether each displacement happens (LO-1) and then demands the balanced equation where it does (C 1.3-LO-1).
Zinc against five reagents: decide where a displacement occurs (LO-1) and write the equations (C 1.3-LO-1). Same two-instruction shape as qid:84851.
Balanced equation in (a); (b) asks for the other name of the reaction, i.e. double displacement, which is LO-1 classification.
Which container holds which solution is decided by whether a displacement or acid attack occurs -- reactivity reasoning under LO-1. Not LO-2: no corrosion product is being described.

Burns and 'why was so much heat evolved' make this an energy-change item, for which this frame has no learning outcome; the 'what values are exhibited' part has no curricular home at all. Competency level rather than a forced LO.
Why a cycle rusted in the open and what rust-proof paint does -- corrosion in everyday life, LO-2.
Black turbidity in a silver nitrate solution left in light is photolytic decomposition inferred from an observation, which is LO-1.
Foul-smelling chips, the cause of spoilage and the nature of the reaction: rancidity, named explicitly in LO-2.
The delayed whiteness is the slow combination of Ca(OH)2 with atmospheric CO2 to give CaCO3, so the student must recognise that combination reaction. The rate aspect has no outcome in this frame.
'What is rust' is the corrosion product of iron -- LO-2's corrosion clause; no reaction is being classified, so LO-1 does not apply.

Pure reactivity-series recall with no reaction given and nothing to observe or write. LO-1 requires identifying a reaction from observations, so the competency is the correct level; this frame has no reactivity-series outcome.
Sorts two given equations into combination and displacement -- LO-1 classification, with no equation to write.
Distinguishes a displacement from a neutralisation (a double displacement). Both categories sit inside LO-1's list, so LO-1 and not C 1.3-LO-1 -- the equations are given.
Which compound is oxidised in H2S + Br2 -- the oxidation clause of LO-1, decided by loss of hydrogen rather than gain of oxygen.
Ways to prevent rancidity (antioxidants, nitrogen flushing) -- LO-2's rancidity clause.
Names metals that resist corrosion, which is the corrosion-of-metals half of LO-2 read from the other direction.
Identifies the oxidised and reduced species in CuO + Zn. Stored concept tag 'Precipitation reaction' is wrong; the tested outcome is redox identification under LO-1.
Detecting rancid cheese by smell and taste -- recognising the everyday effect of oxidation named in LO-2.
Aluminium foil for food turns on the protective oxide layer keeping air and moisture off, i.e. oxidation and its prevention in everyday life.

'What happens chemically' when quick lime meets water -- recognising the combination reaction CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. Cited at LO-1 rather than C 1.2 because a reaction type is genuinely being identified, unlike the purely thermal items in this batch.
Asks only for an example of an exothermic reaction. Energy classification has no learning outcome in this frame, so competency level, consistent with the other exo/endothermic items.
Example of an endothermic reaction -- same frame gap as qid:84871, mapped to the same competency deliberately.
Nitrogen for storing chips -- preventing rancidity, LO-2.
Names the type of N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 as combination. Pure classification; the equation is supplied and already balanced.
Wants a double displacement example (LO-1) supplied 'with complete balanced equation' (C 1.3-LO-1); the parenthesis makes the second outcome explicit.
Decomposition as the reverse of combination -- two of LO-1's named types. This is a verbatim duplicate of qid:84799 in the same chapter.
Identifies what is reduced and what is oxidised in MnO2 + 4HCl -- redox identification, LO-1.
The whole question is 'is there any change in temperature' -- an energy-change observation. No LO covers heat evolved, so competency level.
Bare recall of AgBr and AgCl as the photography salts. Nothing is observed, classified or written, so LO-1 does not fit; the competency covers knowing the substances and their properties.
The chemical change on heating limestone is thermal decomposition -- LO-1's decomposition clause. C 1.3-LO-1 rejected: the equation is a bonus, the named change is the answer.
Three given equations, each to be read for what is oxidised and what is reduced -- LO-1 redox identification.
Four given equations to be sorted into combination, displacement, combustion and decomposition -- LO-1 classification.
Lime water turning milky and then clear with excess CO2: recognising the precipitation of CaCO3 and its redissolution from the observation. LO-1 is the nearest fit; no equation is demanded.
Why a reactive metal is safe for food packing -- the self-limiting oxide layer, an everyday consequence of oxidation, LO-2.
Neutralisation defined and exemplified. This frame lists double displacement in LO-1 and neutralisation is its acid-base case, so LO-1 rather than the competency.
Parts (a) and (c) are pure LO-1 -- combustion as oxidation, and why silver cannot displace hydrogen. Part (b), the pop test for hydrogen, has no outcome in this frame and is not separately cited.
Defines oxidation and then asks which substance is oxidised and which reduced -- LO-1 throughout. The referenced reactions are missing from the stored stem.
Three balanced equations already supplied; the only task is naming the type of each, which is LO-1 and not C 1.3-LO-1.
Two observations of CaO with water plus the name and formula of the product: recognising the combination reaction from what is seen. The temperature rise has no LO of its own.

Stem has lost its sub-questions and states only the scenario, but the chemistry is unambiguously the strongly exothermic slaking of quick lime, an energy-change topic with no learning outcome in this frame. Mapped at competency level; the truncated stem is reported as a defect.
Observation then 'what type of reaction is this' (LO-1) then the balanced equation (C 1.3-LO-1) -- one instruction per outcome.
Colour change of AgCl in sunlight plus 'state the type of chemical reaction' -- decomposition identified from an observation, LO-1 verbatim.
Demands the balanced equation and the reaction type; the rider about physical conditions (both must be aqueous) reinforces C 1.3-LO-1's physical-states clause rather than introducing a third outcome.
Defines redox and then decides whether magnesium is oxidised or reduced from the burning observation -- LO-1's oxidation clause.
Part (b) is an explicit balancing task (C 1.3-LO-1); part (c) asks what a decomposition reaction is (C 1.2-LO-1). Part (a) is the exothermic slaking, which has no LO.

Part (b) 'why is it always essential to balance a chemical equation' is C 1.3-LO-2's conservation-of-mass reasoning; part (d) on rusting in distilled water is C 1.2-LO-2. Parts (a) and (c) -- irreversibility and heats of combustion of allotropes -- have no outcome in this frame.
Four laboratory observations, each to be named as a reaction type. LO-1 is the whole question; no equations are demanded.
Parts (a)-(c) identify X, Y and Z from burning and dissolution observations (LO-1); part (d) demands the chemical reactions (C 1.3-LO-1).
Part (i) accounts for two observations as decomposition and oxidation (LO-1); part (ii) defines three reaction types and asks for balanced equations (C 1.3-LO-1).
Part (a) is a balancing task, part (b) a classification task, part (c) an oxidation identified from a colour change -- C 1.3-LO-1 and C 1.2-LO-1 between them cover all three.
